result.summary: Pindar wishes the centaur Cheiron were alive to heal King Hieron of Syracuse, and tells how Apollo saved Asklepios from the pyre of his mother Koronis. He reflects on mortal limits, the mixed fortunes of Peleus and Kadmos, and the lasting life poetry gives to virtue.

scenes.title: Editor's note on date
scenes.summary: The editor discusses the uncertain date of the ode and its focus on Hieron's illness.

scenes.title: Wish for Cheiron alive
scenes.summary: Pindar wishes Cheiron still lived on Pelion, as the teacher of Asklepios.

scenes.title: Koronis, Apollo and the pyre
scenes.summary: Koronis, pregnant by Apollo, takes another lover; Apollo has Artemis kill her, then snatches the child from the pyre and gives him to Cheiron.
scenes.stakes: Koronis risks death for betraying Apollo; the unborn child risks burning with her.

scenes.title: Asklepios heals and is struck
scenes.summary: Asklepios heals all kinds of ailments but takes gold to raise a man from death, and Zeus kills him with lightning.
scenes.stakes: Asklepios risks divine punishment for overstepping mortal limits.

scenes.title: Pindar's wish to sail to Hieron
scenes.summary: Pindar urges accepting mortal limits and imagines sailing to Syracuse with a healer and a victory song.
scenes.stakes: Hieron's health is at risk from illness.

scenes.title: Fortunes of Peleus and Kadmos
scenes.summary: Even Peleus and Kadmos, blessed at their weddings, later suffered grief.
scenes.stakes: Even the most blessed mortals suffer loss.

scenes.title: Pindar's humble resolve
scenes.summary: Pindar accepts his own portion and says songs give virtue lasting fame, as with Nestor and Sarpedon.

alias_notes.explanation: Title of Apollo as god of oracles.
Cheiron described as the centaur of Magnesia.

notable_quotes.reason: Famous maxim urging acceptance of mortal limits.
Proverb of two evils for one good.

analysis.text: The ode contrasts mortal limits with divine power, warning against seeking immortality while consoling Hieron that even the blessed suffer.
Pindar composed for tyrants like Hieron, offering praise and consolation; here he addresses the ruler's illness through myth.

legacy.text: Asklepios became the Greek god of medicine, and his rod and serpent remains a symbol of medicine today.

fun_facts.text: The horse Pherenikos, whose name means 'victory-bringer', won at both Delphi and Olympia for Hieron.

language_notes.text: "Fain were I" means "I would gladly wish"; the wish is for something impossible, since Cheiron is long dead.
"Anodynes" are pain-relieving remedies; here they are the healing drugs Asklepios learned to devise.
Eileithuia was the goddess of childbirth. Koronis died before she could give birth with her help.
"Phoibos" (Phoebus) is Apollo, whose epithet means "bright"; "unshorn hair" marks him as an eternally youthful god.
"Hymeneal" means of a wedding; Hymenaios was the wedding song sung outside the bridal chamber.
"Loxias" is a title of Apollo as the oracle-god, meaning roughly "the oblique one"; the unerring partner is probably his prophetic power.
"At the first stride" means in a single step, showing the god's immediate, effortless movement.
"Kentaur of Magnes" is Cheiron, a centaur living in Magnesia, the region around Mount Pelion.
"Emollient spells" means soothing, softening incantations; "hung their limbs with charms" refers to tying amulets on the afflicted body parts.
"A man already prisoner thereto" means a man already held fast by death. "The twain" are the healer and the dead man he raised.
"Leto's son" is Apollo, and "her son's sire" is Apollo's father Zeus; the healer sought is Asklepios, Apollo's son.
"The Mother" is Cybele, a mother goddess honoured with Pan by night dances near Pindar's house in Thebes.
"Putting the fair side forward" means showing a brave face, hiding one's misfortunes from others.
"Those daughters" are Kadmos' daughters, whose sufferings included Semele's death by lightning. Thyone is Semele, mother of Dionysus by Zeus.
The "son of Peleus" is Achilles, killed by an arrow at Troy. "Danaoi" is a name for the Greeks.

context_notes.text: Cheiron was the wise centaur who trained heroes, including Achilles and Jason. Asklepios became the god of medicine.
Koronis is the daughter of Phlegyas. Apollo's sister Artemis was a huntress who often killed on his behalf.
Ischys is Koronis's mortal lover. Lakereia was her home town, beside Lake Boibias in Thessaly.
Hephaistos, god of fire, is used here for the fire of the funeral pyre itself.
Asklepios, son of Apollo, was a healer who broke the natural order by raising the dead. Zeus, son of Kronos, killed him with a thunderbolt.
Cheiron was the wise centaur who taught Asklepios medicine. Pindar wishes he were still alive to provide a healer for Hieron, who was ill.
Arethusa was a spring on Ortygia, the island part of Syracuse. Hieron ruled Syracuse and had founded the city of Aitna.
Peleus married the sea goddess Thetis, and Kadmos married Harmonia. Both weddings were attended by gods and Muses.

literary_notes.text: Asklepios is called "gentle deviser of limb-saving anodynes", and Cheiron a "Beast untamed" yet loving, defining each by a trait.
Pindar turns Koronis's act into a general moral about people who scorn what is near and chase distant things.
Her neighbours' deaths with hers are compared to one spark burning a whole forest, showing how one person's guilt spreads.
The flames splitting open before Apollo is a vivid miracle image, showing divine power over death and fire.
Wisdom is spoken of as a captive led off by greed, presenting the moral failing of Asklepios as a defeat.
Pindar's song becomes a shining light, brighter than any star, to compare the poem's glory to heavenly radiance.
The saying of the men of old gives the ode's central teaching: suffering outweighs good in mortal life.
Changing winds stand for the shifting fortunes of human life, which blow differently from time to time.
Fame is imagined as a structure built by skilled craftsmen, comparing poets to builders who make memory last.
